analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 336, the Toilet Goods Association, Inc., the Dow Petitioners v. John W. Gardner, Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare, and number 438, John W. Gardner, Secretary of Health, Education and Welfare v. the Toilet Goods Association. Mr. Lowen. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court. This case, which is here on crosswritz of certiorari to the Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, demonstrates even more clearly than does the Abbott Laboratories case the harms which flow from premature judicial intervention into the administration of the Food and Drug and Cosmetic Act. Under the terms of that statute, as enacted in 1938, the Food and Drug Administration was to protect the nation's consumers against certain harmful coloring ingredients in foods, drugs, and cosmetics by a pre-marketing clearance procedure under which it was to require manufacturers to test coal tar colors for safety. After the Food and Drug Administration had reviewed the results of these tests, it was authorized to list such colors as it found harmless or suitable for use. Late in 1958, this Court sustained the Food and Drug Administration's position that the statutory scheme under that 1938 Act contemplated that only totally harmless coal tar colors could be listed. In other words, thatch firstly took theory ì obe GBPS Cohum Halo glyph тогоoque qualificationsîî 2015 1976 Este finals Recognizing the merit of an industry complaint that such an absolute standard prohibited the use of coloring ingredients which might be totally innocuous in small quantities as actually used, the Food and Drug Administration supported a mandatory legislation which was enacted as the Color Additive Amendments of 1960. That statute, which is reprinted in relevant portions of pages 24 and 29 to 37 of our brief in this case, extended the pre-marketing clearance procedures to all Color Additives, both natural and synthetic, coal tar, and any other coloring ingredients which were derived from any other source. It empowered the Food and Drug Administration, which had been delegated the powers of the Secretary of Health, Education, and Welfare under the Act, to list Color Additives after review of testing information submitted by the manufacturer with, quote, conditions under which the additives might be safely used. Section 706, A2B, and A3, which appear at page 30 of our brief, are quite clear on that subject. They authorized the Secretary to list a color additive for a, quote, more limited use or uses than have been applied for, and to, quote, prescribe the conditions under which such additive may be safely employed for such use or uses. The Act was passed in July of 1960 with appropriate provisions for provisional listings of color additives which had there to be used until the administrative machinery had gone through the process and completed verifying the information on the color additive applications which would be submitted. In June 1963, the Commissioner of Food and Drug, after affording notice and an opportunity to submit written comments under Section 4 of the Administrative Procedure Act, issued substantially the regulations which appear 22 CFR 8.1 to 8.52. It covers about 20 pages in the Code of Federal Regulations. Among those regulations were four clauses which are specifically the challenge in this case. Section 8.1, all those four all appear at pages 37 and 38 of our brief. Section 8.1F defined color additive as used in the statute and has been subjected to these procedures by the Congress to include a, quote, substance that, when applied to the human body, results in coloring. And it specifically enumerated lipstick, rubes, eye makeup colors, and related cosmetics intended for coloring the human body. In other words, the Food and Drug Administration construed the Act as subjecting to this pre-marketing clearance procedure, finished cosmetic products used for coloring the human body. The very same section of color additive also defined color additive to include all diluents. And diluents were defined in the definitionary provisions of that regulation as any component of a color additive mixture that is not of itself a color additive and has been intentionally mixed therein to facilitate the use of the mixture in color. In other words, anything added for purposes of, essentially anything added to a product which contains coloring and greeting. In addition, Section 8.01U defines the hair dye exemption of the statute. The statute, specifically, Congress exempted from its provisions hair dyes, provisions of the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and the pre-clearance procedures, hair dyes which contain color ingredients whose harmful nature could be determined by what's commonly known as a patch test, a test which the consumer could apply to his own skin and determine whether there was anything in that hair dye which would harm him or her. And the Food and Drug Administration in these regulations construe the hair dye exemption of the statute as not applying to any hair dyes containing products whose harmful effects could not be tested by a patch test. It was going behind the words of the statute to the purpose of Congress. And finally, the fourth provision involved in this suit, and the one in which the Food and Drug Administration was sustained by the Court of Appeals, warned that if employees of the Food and Drug Administration were denied access to manufacturing facilities, processes, or formulae of drugs, of cosmetics which they were required to certificate, and in effect by that certification to check the very product itself, then the commissioner might immediately suspend the certification service, thereby making those products non-marketable. That was in July of 1963. In November of that year, before the regulations were put in effect and before compliance with any of these regulations, or before in effect these procedures had been gone through, this action to declare those regulations invalid was instituted. The district judge first denied a motion to dismiss in November of 1964, and then after the Abbott Laboratories case was decided by the Third Circuit in December of 1965, he certified interlocutory appeal under 28 U.S.C. 1292-B on that issue as to whether this suit was premature or was right at this juncture or not. The Court of Appeals affirmed the district judge's refusal to dismiss the first three counts of the complaint, but concluded that the fourth count, attacking the factory inspection provision, was premature and should be dismissed. So the only issue before this court, really, the only issue before the Court of Appeals on the interlocutory appeal, was the question of rightness and prematurity. In this case, unlike Abbott Laboratories, we do not alternatively urge, for that reason, that the Court's decision of the merits. We do not go on to discuss or urge the merits beyond the jurisdictional point, because we think the only issue that was properly before the Court of Appeals on the interlocutory appeal was the question of prematurity and rightness. I noticed the parties took pretrial discovery. They took about a year for pretrial discovery. What were the issues? Do you enlighten me about that, as to which they took pretrial testimony? Well, I know that the district judge, I think, was concerned over the intent of the people who were behind the legislation. I'm really not sure as to what the pretrial discovery concerns about, apparently, the intent, the motives, the legislative intent behind the statute. Had to do with legislative history, as I read the briefs, that they interviewed people who were there at the committee hearings. Yes, the district judge thought that was a relevant way of determining what the statute meant. I don't know whether all, I suppose, I'm told, that all the pretrial discovery concerned that issue. What did the legislators intend when they passed the color ad with amendment? We don't necessarily agree that that's a proper way of determining legislative intent, I must say, but that was the district judge's view. Now, we've attempted in the introduction to our main brief and in our reply brief to explain why we think that this case, in its present posture, at least insofar as it affects those first two counts, the finished cosmetic products and the diluents, is particularly premature and entirely hypothetical. I'll try to summarize that position as briefly as I can. It appears to be agreed, and I don't think there can be any question whatsoever, that under the 1960 amendments, the color additive amendments to the Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, Congress intended that the Food and Drug Administration apply a safety and use standard under which the administration was to determine, before listing a color additive, not whether that color additive in the abstract and just taken purely by itself was safe, but whether as used in a finished cosmetic or in any finished product, whether that color ingredient was safe. Consequently, the practical result of the administration of that kind of a test is that an applicant for listing doesn't satisfy his burden under the statute by merely testing the color ingredient as such, just that pigment. He has to submit to the commissioner information on how he will use the coloring ingredient and sufficient scientific data, pre-testing, if you will, as to the other ingredients that will be included with the pigment or the dye and the finished product. In other words, the Food and Drug Administration cannot be expected, in administering a safety and use standard, to list color X as safe for use in a finished product unless it has adequate information that the finished product and the ingredients that are added to the color pigment or dye are safe for use. Well, if that's true, that an entirely pigment or dye that may appear to be safe in the abstract when combined with other products or when put in a finished product may not be safe for listing, then obviously the Commissioner of Food and Drugs, the Food and Drug Administration, when it finally lists color X for safe in use in a certain finished product, is in effect listing the finished product as well as the coloring ingredient. And that's the kind of thing which becomes obvious we submit once this whole system, as administered by the Food and Drug Administration, goes into effect. If the companies in this case were to submit adequate information under a safety and use standard, even under their own construction of what color additive means, and if the Food and Drug Administration were then to find that those pigments, those coloring ingredients, as used in a finished product, are safe and are listable, in effect, and will be listed, then the controversy is over. They haven't been heard at all. Their finished product will be listed, their coloring ingredient will be listed, and their diluents will be listed. I thought their point was that you don't have jurisdiction to list or not list or control or have they have anything to say about their finished product as such, as such. Well, we think, we submit that they, and I don't think they really dispute it, is that we have jurisdiction, or the Food and Drug Administration has jurisdiction to control a finished product, although not as such, if it had no coloring ingredient, but does have jurisdiction to control it as the terminal use of a coloring ingredient. Well, that is precisely what makes this suit, that's the first two counts, disappear, we think, because if we do have jurisdiction to make that determination, then they're very likely not to be heard at all once the whole machinery has been carried through. And that, it seems to me, indicates to us what the harms are, or is illustrative of the harms of premature judicial intervention. And how about the diluent, diluent, how do you pronounce it? The diluent. We think that that's true of the diluents, too. Assuming you take a coloring ingredient that's totally harmless in and of itself, if it, combined with any other product in which it appears in a finished cosmetic product, produces a poisonous result because the diluent is poisonous, obviously the commissioner can't be expected to list the coloring ingredient as permissible for use with that diluent. And the statute itself makes entirely clear that the listings are supposed to list the coloring ingredients for use with or without certain diluents. Now, if that's true, and the commissioner is supposed to specify the diluents with which pigment X can be mixed, well, then he's got to pass on whether the diluents are safe. And the way he passes on that is he asks the requires of these companies to make tests on their diluents, to submit the results of those tests, and to have the Food and Drug Administration pass upon them. So that although this suit at the present time may look like a challenge to the Food and Drug Administration's regulation, if, in fact, you waited until the companies actually felt any kind of pinch at all, I think it'd be discovered that they'd feel none. Now, they say... I thank you, pardon me. I thought that they were contending that the commissioner says, I'm going to list and certify the diluents separately. The commissioner, Mr. Justin Sporters, I don't think has ever said that. And from what I understand, the Food and Drug Administration takes no such position. Its position is that you can list products, either, let's say, lipsticks, either under a common base, under a common coloring ingredient. You can list it together with certain diluents, list the diluents separately. But there's nothing in the statute, and there's nothing in the Food and Drug Administration's administration of these provisions, which would require them to list these separately. And that, we think, also explodes the exaggerated costs claim. There are mammoth estimates because of one affidavit in the record, and that also appear in the brief of the companies in this case, as to the costs of complying with this because of the listing and testing provisions. Well, the listing, there is a listing deposit under the regulations issued by the Food and Drug Administration of $2,600 per petition for listing. But that's a deposit only. That's to defray the processing course of the Food and Drug Administration and passing on the petition. Now, the Food and Drug Administration is not going to be listing or incurring this $2,600 cost with each one of the lipsticks of any of the particular plaintiffs, obviously. They can list them all together under one paragraph of the Code of Federal Regulation, and the total costs will not even remotely approach what the plaintiffs in this case contain. And the same thing is true with the pre-testing. Sure, there would have to be testing of the finished product and of the diluents. But there are so many common ingredients among all these. I mean, the plaintiffs refer to one company's 2,700 cosmetic formulae. But there are so many common ingredients, let's say, among all of these lipsticks, that it's fallacious to just simply multiply them all and say that gives you the total cost of complying with the Food and Drug Administration's regulations. Do you think this case, then, is quite different from the one we just heard, Abbott? Well, we think it's more premature, if you could put it that way. Well, because I understood you in the Abbott case. You said there was really no question about the complete lack of ambiguity, the clarity and certainty of the meaning of the regulation there involved. And that in that sense, at least, while you used your word abstract, it really wasn't abstract. It was, its meaning was clear. Yes. Its meets and bounds were clear. Yes. And here you say this is not. So. That's right. Well, I think maybe the way to distinguish the two... Or at least the arguing about the meaning. Right. Well, the way to distinguish... And in Abbott, there was no argument at all about the meaning. I think the way to distinguish the two is that in Abbott labs, you know exactly what the plaintiffs will have to do to comply with the regulations. Yes. In this case, we submit it's very likely they'll have to do nothing more than they would have to do anyway to comply with these regulations. Well, of course, they disagree with you. But in that respect, this case is different in the end that you do disagree as to the meaning of the regulations. Is that true? I don't know whether you could put that as to the meaning of the regulations. I think it's more as to the effect. Or the impact of the impact. The impact of the regulations. Yes. I think there is that. Now, the plaintiffs in this case, as well as the plaintiffs in Abbott lab, talk about their harms in terms of publicity as a result of seizure or injunctive suits or criminal prosecutions. Well, again, that's precisely the harm which this court referred to in the Mighty Urine-Castleberry case. And in an opinion by Mr. Justice Douglas said that in the context of the Food and Drug Act, that the fact that a seizure might cause irreparable harm to a business didn't mean, quote, that the hand of government must be stayed until the courts have an opportunity to determine whether the government is justified in instituting suit. That was a preliminary step to a seizure. And this is an even more preliminary step, in effect, to a seizure, because this is, in effect, the Commission saying, the Food and Drug Administration saying, that these are the procedural steps we will go through, or these are the requirements we will impose on the industry before we ultimately pass on all these, all the color additive, the safety of the color additive. Mr. Lewin, if an individual manufacturer, after appropriate procedure, challenged this in a particular case, as you argue is contemplated by statute, would it be possible for him to argue that the regulation is confiscatory? I think he could. I don't, I don't, the President can see in what way... Well, they now, in this case, don't they, in paragraph 47 of their complaint, as I see it, they're arguing, making a kind of a substantive due process argument, that this regulation is confiscatory on an industry-wide basis, which does sound to me like a sort of a substantive due process attack, but on an industry-wide basis, in other words, the industry as a whole says we're entitled to be considered as a whole, and considering us as a whole, this regulation is confiscatory. Well, I think paragraph 47 goes to the fee requirement again, Mr. Justin. Close to it. To the fee requirement. Yes, to the fee requirement. In other words, what they're saying, in effect, is that the total fees which result from requiring separate listing is confiscatory. Well, it goes back to the separate listing point. That's right. And I was just wondering what comment you have to make as to what seems to me, perhaps erroneously, to be the basic theory underlying this case, and perhaps remotely and indirectly the preceding case, and that is that an industry as a whole has a standing to challenge a government regulation, and that the industry as a whole in this particular paragraph has a standing to have the economic impact of a regulation considered on the industry as a whole for the purpose of determining whether it's confiscatory. I think there are really two answers I'd have to that, Mr. Justin. First, there's nothing in what the plaintiffs here or an Abbott Labs urge which would limit their suit to an industry-wide suit as a whole. If in some way there were some means of ensuring that an entire industry would bring a suit which would protect that industry's interest, I think it would take a statute myself. But if there was some way of limiting the doctrine of that, then I think the questions would be substantially different. And one of our problems with the rightness claim, in this case and in Abbott Labs, is that it opens the doors to individual suits. I think a second answer is really that neither in Abbott Labs, certainly, where whatever claim the whole industry has, the individual drug manufacturer has as well, nor in this case, where there's really no basis for the claim, can there be any industry-wide claim. Let me see if I can make that last point a little bit clearer, really. If it were true that the Food and Drug Administration regulations prescribed an absolute $2,600 fee for each listing, and the Food and Drug Administrator Commissioner said, I will have to list every finished cosmetic product separately. That's the way I construe it. And I won't allow you to do anything other than that. I think there might be room to argue that the harm that would be done by waiting until the actual pinch is felt would be irreparable, because the industry would be expected to forego for $2,600 for each of... Well, would that support this lawsuit? Pardon? Assuming that what you say were true, would they have a right-turn injunction? I think... Could this... Would they have a standing to maintain this, or would this be an appropriate suit? Well, I think there would be... I think there'd be much more basis for permitting that kind of a suit. We think... We think, and I think we've tried to make clear in our brief, that rightness is not something that you can determine simply by any actual rules. We think that when, really, a whole industry may be hurt, or will be hurt, by being forced to pay confiscatory costs, which they will have no opportunity to litigate at any later time. In other words, the regulation either has to be challenged now or never. We think that would be right. Well, why can't they be litigated at a later time? If this can be, why couldn't they refuse to list and go ahead and market the product and have action brought against them of one sort or another, and then contend, in defense of their listing, that the payment of the fee was confiscatory? Well, and that would be true of that individual fee, Mr. Justice Ford, but if their allegations are true, I suppose, they say we've already paid... we've been forced to pay $7 million with all our 2,700 petitions. And to force us to pay $7 million... If you're willing to concede that, I have difficulty with the rest of your ideas. Well, I'm not prepared to concede it, but I'm saying that's a different... it seems that that's a different case. If that were true, I think this case might be closer to Abbott Laboratories. The fact that that isn't true, I think, is what makes this case disappear, makes it much clearer than Abbott Laboratories, because in this case, there's no such requirement. The industry is not being asked today to pay $42 million in listing fees or forego using its cosmetics for the next few years. If that were true, we think there might be some room for arguing that maybe they ought to be permitted to litigate that case. Mr. Ross? Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court. The basic distinction between the cosmetic case and the Abbott Laboratories case has not really been set forth yet. And this is the distinction. In Abbott Laboratories, Congress did, in fact, legislate a requirement that there be prominence to the generic name. And the issue was whether or not the regulations properly implemented a power which was granted to the agency. And that's probably why their complaint alleges the unreasonableness of the regulations. This is not the kind of issue in our case. Our case is one where Congress never granted the power to the agency. The agency, arrogated to itself, it took new and different powers from those which Congress granted. In fact, it took powers which it requested of Congress and which Congress refused to grant by declining to enact the legislation which would have accomplished the power which was ultimately taken by the regulations. except in degree there, what's the difference? The question is is the power of the agency to do what it did under the statute, isn't it? Well, it's a question of degree but a very substantial degree. What it was done here, Your Honor, was to subject an industry which was not subject to getting a license before it could sell its products to getting a license. Now, before any finished cosmetic product which imparts a color to the body may be sold, that product must be pre-cleared by FDA and there must be a license for it. And the statute doesn't require this kind of a license. It requires a license for one ingredient, the color which was added to the product, not for the entire product. Now, the hair dye allegation illustrates this very clearly. The statute says that hair dyes are exempt. They're exempt if they bear a certain kind of label which is very specifically provided for by the statute. The exemption is so complete that even the provision with respect to clearing the color ingredients says if it is not a hair dye so that the color in the hair dye doesn't have to be cleared by the agency. Nevertheless, the agency rewrote the statute, changed its provisions, and said from now on the entire hair dye product must be pre-cleared by the Food and Drug Administration. It may not be sold unless it gets this prior license. It may not be sold unless we list it in a regulation, and this listing means setting forth the specifications and formula of the product, although these are trade secrets. They must be published in the Federal Register for all competitors to see and copy if they want, and then certifying the batches. Now, these are substantially new and substantially different powers from those which were intended to be given the agency by Congress. and the proof of it lies in the fact that on repeated occasions, FDA-sponsored legislation in which it urged that it was desirable to impose this kind of a license on finished cosmetic products. Innumerable bills were introduced for the pre-clearance of cosmetics, and these were never enacted, in some cases after hearings, as to the necessity of this legislation. There were several bills introduced to eliminate the statutory exemption for hair dyes. They were not enacted. There was legislation introduced to give the Food and Drug Administration access to the formulas of all products covered by the Act. And Congress examined this very critically and enacted a provision that they would have access only to the formulas of prescription drugs and not to the formulas of non-prescription drugs or the formulas of cosmetics or the formulas of foods or the formulas of devices. Now, this is the kind of arrogation of power to an agency which has always been reviewable. As early as Stark v. Wicked, this court held that it was an inherent judicial function by injunction in equity to challenge this type of excessive power. And the only time it could not be challenged if there was a specific provision in a statute which prevented challenge. They said mere silence was not sufficient. This was the decision in the frozen food case where this court will recall it said that what was being done there was to license an industry or require licensing for an industry where the act did require it. And it was allowed to be challenged in equity by an injunction action. And it's the very classic kind of a case for which the declaratory judgments law is designed. Because what the Food and Drug Administration is saying, if you don't believe these regulations are valid, ignore them. And then face the penalties of being wrong or even face the penalties of being right. Because as Mr. Giselle said, the headlines that cosmetics which are carefully tested and as to which the companies are very jealous of their reputation and goodwill, there were headlines of multiple seizures because the products were adulterated. This would ruin the industry. Now, in this field, you can have multiple seizures because we're not dealing with the matter of labeling. We're dealing with products which will be called adulterated in the public press if they are sold without complying with a license provision which we assert in the complaint is illegal. Mr. Ross, I suppose the Food and Drug Administration discovered, or thought it discovered, that a particular and common ingredient used in cosmetics caused cancer or induced cancer, giving a wild example. And let's suppose that under 361 pay, after appropriate proceedings, it adopted a regulation saying that cosmetics should be deemed to be adulterated if they include such and such an ingredient, you see, or if the label doesn't say so and so. Now, under your theory of the keys, would an injunction apply? Could a drug cosmetic company or the industry or group cosmetic companies maintain an injunction proceeding to prevent food and drugs from administering that section? I'm not sure, Your Honor. That's a key question, though, isn't it? No, I don't believe it is, because if you're dealing with a question of the propriety of listing the color... No, I'm not. I'm not dealing with that. I'm dealing with the question of court jurisdiction. Now, I'm talking about Section 361, which is your section here. If I understand your question correctly, you're saying that if FDA were to determine that a particular color ingredient... Not color ingredient, just ingredients. Oh, any ingredient? Any ingredient. I don't know of any provision they would have to... Well, I'm going about 361A. ...to pre... They could... If it were adulterated, then the product could be seized after sale. There is a post-marketing power after sale. There is no pre-marketing clearance of cosmetics. There is a pre-marketing clearance of dye... I understand. I would suppose the secretary adopted a promulgated regulation, and he said that these cosmetics shall not contain this ingredient, or shall not contain this ingredient unless there is a warning on the label. That's under 361. And I just... I want to know whether industry or company, if it thought that that was confiscatory, might very well be in practical effect, could bring an injunction proceeding. I would think that would be a classic case where the expertise of the agency would be involved. And any court... Well, didn't the district court here say that expert testimony would be helpful? Well, it did. Principally in connection with the legislative history. They wanted to have testimony as to what type of technical problem was involved, and particularly testimony from those who helped shape the legislative history. But just to finish my answer to your question, Your Honor, when you're dealing with the question of the safety or propriety of a particular ingredient, that is a matter for the special competence or expertise of the Food and Drug Administration. administration. And normally, I would say that the proper procedure would be to go before the agency, have your evidentiary hearing, obtain your findings, and then appeal to the Court of Appeals based upon that record. The reason I express doubt is because in connection with this case, for the first time, I heard the government say that the saving clause in the statute is not a broad saving clause as the courts below held and as I always understood it to be, but was a saving clause to give two remedies for the type of case that involved this administrative hearing. They say in their brief, and it was said on the oral argument, that the saving clause applies only to those proceedings for which the administrative procedure applies, and it's an additional remedy. It doesn't apply to a remedy such as we have sought here. And that came as a surprise to me, which is why I said I was doubtful as to what the answer was. But normally, I would say this is the type of proceeding that goes before an administrative agency with administrative hearings involving the special competence and expertise of the agency with direct appeal to the Court of Appeals. But this is, of course, not the issue with respect to whether the statute goes as far as these regulations. And I might note that this is conceded by the government because in their brief, they say if they are wrong as to the reviewability feature, they don't think any evidence is needed for a trial, and the record as it now stands is sufficient for the Court to adjudicate this issue of statutory interpretation. But by contrast with the Abbott case, the government is not asking us to adjudicate the merits. No, they're not. If we think they're wrong, it is asking us not to. That's correct. What they are saying is the District Court was wrong in denying my motion for summary judgment, which was opposed by the government. And they say the District Court could now determine these as questions of law without the necessity of any further evidence. And as I point out in the brief, where in fact someone filed objections before the administrative agency and to a different regulation and urged as a ground for objection that there was no authority in the statute, they refused to accept these objections for filing and said they raised issues of law which couldn't be covered in an administrative hearing, which is exactly our position on this case. I'd like briefly to answer Mr. Lewin's argument with respect to the rightness feature. It is based, in my judgment, on a misreading of the regulations. The regulations apply now. The statute is very plain. It says that if something is a color additive, it must now be listed and certified by the Food and Drug Administration. So anything which the regulation defines to be a color additive requires this license before it may be sold. The regulations say in their definitions that a diluent is a color additive. And therefore it follows that the diluent must now be listed and must now be subject to certification. The regulations further say that lipstick, rouge, eye makeup colors, and all related cosmetics for coloring the body are color additives. These color additives, if they are color additives, a license is now required. A listing petition must be presented, which must be accompanied by the $2,600 fee. Now, in the discovery proceedings, which we had to try to clarify the intent of this regulation, it was very clearly testified to by the Deputy Commissioner of Food and Drug Administration, with reference to this 2,700 cosmetics of Colma Laboratories, that if, as we assert, each one is a different formula, that a separate petition would have to be filed for each of these 2,700 cosmetics, and a separate fee of $2,600 would be payable. Was that the thrust of the pretrial to find out the purpose of the regulations? Well, the thrust was multiple.
